title: Tisha B'Av: Lamentations
hook: read by candlelight, sitting low; the Talmud says the second Temple fell for baseless hatred (Yoma 9b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fast that opens three weeks between the narrow places. Your line was walls breached. Three weeks later, the fire.

Evening, in a synagogue, on the ninth of Av. The big lights are off or turned low. In many places the curtain has been taken down from the ark. People wear sneakers or cloth shoes, because leather is set aside for the day. Nobody greets anyone. They sit on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at home. Someone has a candle, someone a phone flashlight. Then a reader begins a slow, falling chant, and the first word is a cry.
screen: `THE LIGHTS GO LOW.` → `NO LEATHER, NO GREETINGS.` → `EVERYONE SITS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Eicha means how, the how you say when you can't believe what you're seeing. It's the first word of Lamentations, and Jews call the whole book by it. The old Jewish translation opens: "How doth the city sit solitary." Jerusalem, once full of people, sits alone like a widow. Of the book's five chapters, four are built on the alphabet, verse by verse, as if grief needed every letter there is. Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the day the tradition remembers both Temples falling, the first to Babylon, the second to Rome, centuries apart, mourned on one day. It's a full fast, from sunset to the next nightfall. Anyone who is ill, pregnant, nursing, or whose health would be at risk asks a doctor and a rabbi, and Jewish law puts protecting life first. Then the mourner's question: why? The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, gives a stinging answer. The first Temple fell because of idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed. But in the second Temple's time, people studied Torah, kept the commandments and did acts of kindness. So why did it fall? Sinat chinam, baseless hatred: hatred for no reason worth the name. And baseless hatred, it says, weighs as much as those three sins together. The rabbis didn't only blame the empire with the battering rams. They looked at their own community: the feuds, the contempt, the neighbor nobody would speak to. And the book doesn't end in the dark. Its last chapter asks God to turn us back and renew our days as of old, and because the very last verse is so bitter, the congregation says that line again.
screen: `EICHA: HOW?` · `TWO TEMPLES, ONE DAY OF MOURNING.` · `NOT ONLY ROME: BASELESS HATRED.` · `SAY THE HOPEFUL LINE AGAIN.` · then, large: `BASELESS HATRED DESTROYS.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit low, on the floor or a step, and let one grudge come to mind, the kind that isn't about anything big anymore: an old slight, a neighbor you decided long ago not to like. You don't have to forgive the unforgivable or call anyone; just, for this minute, set this one down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor.
Eicha. How: the first word and the Hebrew name of Lamentations, read on Tisha B'Av, sitting low. Today's word.
Your line: baseless hatred destroys. A day on the floor, asking why out loud. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations chanted in a dim synagogue, followed by kinot, poems of mourning.

chat.says: What does the Talmud say made the Second Temple fall?
options: Baseless hatred: people studied and did kindness, yet hated each other for nothing.
Idolatry, since by then the people had stopped studying the Torah at all.
Only Rome's army; the rabbis taught that the people bore no blame.

notes: Added 2026-10-06 from the five-year map (standing rule: every fast-day lesson carries the health line; never present fasting as required at risk to health): one sentence that health and life come first. Minor fasts (Tenth of Tevet, Fast of Esther, Seventeenth of Tammuz): the ill, pregnant and nursing are generally excused (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 550:1 and 686:2 with commentaries). Tisha B'Av: the ill and anyone at risk eat; others ask a doctor and a rabbi (OC 554:5-6). Confirm with the Keeper.
Quoted Lamentations 1:1 opening phrase as in JPS 1917 ('How doth the city sit solitary'); verify capitalization and wording.
Yoma 9b paraphrased: first Temple for idolatry, forbidden relations, bloodshed; second for sinat chinam, which is equal to the three. Verify.
Customs (no leather shoes, sitting on floor/low stools, no greetings, dimmed lights, removing the parochet in some communities) vary; check phrasing.
Chapters 1, 2, 4 are single acrostics; chapter 3 is a triple acrostic; chapter 5 is not an acrostic. Some chapters reverse ayin and pe.
Repeating 5:21 after 5:22 so the reading ends on hope: a widespread custom; verify.
Tisha B'Av runs about 25 hours, sunset to the following nightfall.
